• Common name: Pygmy chain sword
  • Other names: Helanthium tenellum, Narrow leaf chain sword, Dwarf Amazon sword, Micro Sword
  • Minimum tank size: 40 litres
  • Lighting: moderate to high
  • Water hardness: soft to moderately hard
  • Substrate: needed (nutrient-rich)
  • Growth rate: moderate to high
  • Placement: mostly foreground / midground
  • Leaf size: up to 10 cm
  • Fertilizer: recommended
  • CO2: not needed
  • Propagation: vegetatively by runners (submersed form)

Pygmy chain sword is a marsh plant in the water plantain family Alismataceae. It is native to the Americas: in North America in states such as Texas, Michigan, Florida and Missouri, and in parts of Central and South America (Brazil, Paraguay, Guyana and Argentina), where it grows fully or partially submerged in marshes, ponds, streams and other water bodies.

A fast-growing, tolerant plant that suits beginners; it needs ample light and fertilizer. Add root tabs to the substrate and dose liquid fertilizer sparingly in the water column. Prune overgrown shoots and excess runners regularly to keep the carpet in shape. Dose macronutrients and trace elements such as iron and manganese to prevent deficiencies that discolour the stems. Perform partial water changes weekly.

Planting and propagation: divide a bunch into small clumps by hand and plant them 3–5 cm deep in the substrate, spaced out for better coverage; tweezers help avoid damage. Provide strong light and place root tabs in the substrate. Runners give rise to daughter plants that can be clipped and replanted. Runners may jump out of the substrate, so the plant cannot be kept in one spot. Emersed plants produce seeds freely, but not submersed plants. It suits the dry start method.

Problems:

  • Emersed to submersed: leaves melt during the transition, after which the plant establishes and sends out runners.
  • Relocation: the root system is large, so removing the plant can pull up much of the substrate.
  • Algae: leaves attract algae under excessive light. Reduce light intensity or photoperiod, dose liquid carbon, or add algae-eating fish and invertebrates.
  • Yellowing leaves: mostly caused by iron deficiency; use an iron supplement made for aquarium plants.

Temperature: 22–26°C is optimal for growth. Cooler water is tolerated but may hamper runner formation.

pH: 6.5–7.5.

Hardness: tolerant of a wide range, from soft to hard water.

Tank size: not recommended for nano tanks because of its relatively fast growth; minimum 40 litres.

Lighting: moderate to high light with full-spectrum bulbs. The plant stays smaller under high light and slightly taller under moderate light; strong light gives a reddish tint. Keep the photoperiod up to 12 hours a day, otherwise the carpet becomes sparse.

Substrate: a heavy root-feeder that needs a nutrient-rich substrate. In sand or fine gravel, add root tabs. Recommended: ADA Amazonia aqua soil, CaribSea Eco-Complete, Seachem Fluorite.

CO2 and fertilizers: can grow without CO2 injection, but fertilizing is necessary. Liquid fertilizers rich in macronutrients and iron, plus root tabs, keep it healthy. If keeping shrimp, note that high CO2 and copper (found in most fertilizers) are extremely dangerous to them.

Echinodorus tenellus is the smallest species of the genus Echinodorus, 5–10 cm tall with thin leaves about 3 mm wide. The emersed form has petioles about 7 cm long, each topped with a lanceolate leaf about 2.5 cm long, and produces an umbel of white flowers about 3.5 mm across. Grown submersed, it loses the petioles and produces narrow, pointed leaves up to 10 cm long, olive green, purple or reddish depending on light intensity. It propagates by runners that spread over the bottom to form a lawn. Common forms are the standard variety and E. tenellus 'parvulum', with lighter green, wider leaves.

It is often confused with and sold as Dwarf Sagittaria (Sagittaria subulata), which grows up to 15 cm, has wider leaves (about 5 mm) and is bright light green.

Benefits: a ground-cover plant that gives shelter to bottom-dwelling fish, fry and shrimp, a spawning medium for egg scatterers, a place for biofilm to grow, absorbs excess nutrients, and its roots help break up anaerobic pockets in the substrate.

Tankmates: keep with peaceful fish and invertebrates such as neon tetras, danios, cherry barbs, otocinclus, dwarf shrimp and snails. Avoid fish that eat plants or dig, such as goldfish, koi, oscars and African cichlids, and crayfish and crabs.

Quarantine the plant before adding it, as it may carry parasites, pest snails or pesticide residues that are toxic to shrimp and fish.
